## Chapter Summary

The accounting profession is undergoing a fundamental shift in the skills it demands from practitioners. The growth of transaction data, the spread of automation and artificial intelligence, and the expansion of the accountant's role from preparer to analyst have created strong demand for data analytics competencies. Professional bodies including the AICPA, NASBA, IMA, and IAESB have responded by building analytics and technology into their curricula, examinations, and competency frameworks, signaling that these skills are essential rather than optional.

Analytics in accounting takes four forms. Descriptive analytics summarizes historical data to explain what happened. Diagnostic analytics investigates why it happened by drilling into details and decomposing results into their drivers. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast future outcomes. Prescriptive analytics recommends actions by optimizing objectives subject to constraints. Most accounting analytics work is descriptive, diagnostic, or predictive, and doing this work well requires both technical skill and professional judgment. Each type appears in financial accounting, managerial accounting, and auditing, the three perspectives around which the applied exercises in this book are organized.

Every analytics project follows a consistent workflow. The accountant defines the question, accesses the data, prepares and cleans the data, analyzes it, visualizes the results, and communicates findings. This workflow provides the organizing thread for the entire book.

This book teaches accounting analytics using three complementary tools. SQL is strongest for extracting and combining data from relational databases, Excel for preparation, analysis, and modeling, and Power BI for interactive visualization and communication. All three are applied to the Charles River Accounting Dataset, a single integrated database organized into table groups that correspond to the company's business processes, with source-to-ledger traceability in the GLEntry table designed to connect each posting to the business event that created it. The book introduces the table groups progressively, starting with the Order-to-Cash and Accounting Core groups in the Excel chapters of Part II, expanding into Procure-to-Pay and Manufacturing in the SQL chapters of Part III, building cross-group models in Power BI in Part IV, and integrating all groups in the applied projects of Part V.
